project_name: Pinecrest Mill kraft lignin cake (fictional): dashboard assessment
disclaimers: Fictional demo data: the Pinecrest Mill and this lignin stream are invented. All values are illustrative assumptions, not measurements from any real mill, and must be replaced with a mill's own lab data before any decision.
BioValue AI gives indicative decision support. It does not guarantee profitability, does not verify customer demand, and does not constitute engineering approval.

Gross margin, profitability, NPV, and IRR are not calculated. They need capital costs, fixed costs, a discount rate, a time horizon, and agreed definitions, none of which are available yet. Gross contribution excludes capital costs, fixed costs, and the value of the feedstock in its current use.
Scores use a 1-5 scale. A criterion that was not assessed lowers data completeness; it is never counted as a low score.
1 piece(s) of input or evidence text read like instructions to the AI and were replaced before the agents saw them (see the execution trace).

constraints: The stream is currently routed to internal fuel, so diverting it to a sale or processing pathway would require changing its current use.
There is no lignin dryer; buyers requiring dry powder would need drying capability upstream or downstream.
The lignin is delivered as wet cake, so moisture affects shipped mass and dry-tonnage availability; the recorded moisture is uncertain.
Fractionation and chemical-modification equipment are unavailable, limiting on-site preparation for pathways that require those steps.
Missing molecular-weight, phenolic-hydroxyl, and sodium measurements limit pathway and ash-specification screening.
The record gives covered cake storage but no capacity detail beyond the stated record, so storage and handling may constrain accumulation.
data_quality_notes: This is a fictional demo record; all values are illustrative assumptions, not measured mill data, and should not be used for a real investment decision.
The annual wet quantity, moisture, and composition figures include assumed ranges and variability rather than verified operating data.
The lignin-content analytical method is stated for illustration and needs confirmation for buyer comparisons.
Moisture is marked uncertain and should be confirmed with representative mill measurements.
Molecular weight, phenolic hydroxyl content, and sodium are not measured; sodium information is needed to characterize ash-related requirements.
Validation reports that the dry-matter balance and composition total checks passed, and that each missing figure has a corresponding data-gap entry.
agent.summary: Fictional washed softwood kraft lignin cake profile: 40,000 t/yr wet feedstock, 35.0000000000000003% moisture fraction, and 26,000 t/yr calculated dry mass. Validation found no inconsistencies, but three composition properties are missing and all feedstock figures are illustrative assumptions.

supported_claims.EV-PF-01#1: For kraft lignin in phenol-formaldehyde (PF) resins, the typical replacement of phenol is up to 50%, using a two-step process with depolymerized lignin (Mw 800-1,700 g/mol).
supported_claims.EV-PF-01#2: Kraft lignin needs an activation or depolymerization step before use in PF resins.
supported_claims.EV-PF-01#R1: Pre-treatment of kraft lignin: Activation or depolymerization is needed before kraft lignin is used in PF resins.
supported_claims.EV-PF-02#2: UPM states that LPF resin is industrially proven and meets EN 314-2 Bonding Class 3 for veneer plywood.
supported_claims.EV-PF-02#3: UPM reports formaldehyde emissions (EN 717-2) of 0.230 mg/m²/h for 12 mm spruce, 0.148 for 12 mm birch, and 0.170 for 12 mm combi panels made with LPF resin.
supported_claims.EV-PF-04#2: With the depolymerized lignin making up 50% of the phenolic component, the resin's viscosity, bonding strength, and free formaldehyde met the Chinese wood-adhesive standard used in the study.
supported_claims.EV-PF-01#4: Global PF resin production was expected to reach about 10 Mt (valued at about USD 13.36 billion in 2019), and more than 50% of these resins are used to make adhesives for wood-based panels.

applications.statement: Kraft lignin can partially replace phenol in phenol-formaldehyde resins for plywood and other wood-panel adhesives, but activation or depolymerization may be needed first.

Lignin-phenol-formaldehyde resin is described by UPM as industrially proven for veneer plywood and meeting EN 314-2 Bonding Class 3; the same vendor reports formaldehyde-emission test results under EN 717-2.
A laboratory study also tested kraft-lignin resin in poplar plywood and assessed viscosity, bonding strength, and free formaldehyde against a Chinese wood-adhesive standard.

target_customers.statement: Plywood and other wood-based panel producers are the implied customers for lignin-based PF adhesives.

competing_materials.statement: Phenol in conventional phenol-formaldehyde resin is the material lignin is proposed to replace.

qualification_requirements.statement: Kraft lignin requires activation or depolymerization before PF-resin use.
The vendor reports veneer-plywood bonding performance against EN 314-2 Bonding Class 3 and formaldehyde emissions measured under EN 717-2.
A laboratory study assessed resin properties against a Chinese wood-adhesive standard, whose designation is inconsistent within the paper.

limitations: The strongest commercial-performance and cost statements include vendor technical literature; the cited vendor document gives no test report, and its lignin is not identified as kraft lignin.
The oxidative-depolymerization work is a laboratory study using poplar plywood samples, and the paper names its Chinese standard inconsistently.
The reported general biobased-resin TRL is based on a 2018 source and is not specific to kraft lignin; the review's replacement levels summarize studies rather than one commercial plant.
The review's global production figure is an undated forecast and its market-value figure is from 2019; the reported cost-saving calculation uses past prices.
missing_information: Current regional demand, lignin purchase prices, market volumes accessible to Pinecrest, named buyers, contracts, and buyer qualification timelines are not established.
The evidence does not establish that Pinecrest's wet cake meets the relevant process or product specifications, nor does it provide a commercial-scale qualification result for this feedstock.

market_evidence.rationale: Evidence includes a vendor-described industrially proven plywood resin and product-standard performance, exceeding research-only interest. It does not document lignin-resin sales or multiple established buyers, so the evidence does not support the higher rubric levels.

supported_claims.EV-PU-01#1: Replacing 30 wt% of the petroleum-based polyol with unmodified lignin, 16 of the 19 lignins tested gave rigid PUR/PIR foams that passed all measured ASTM C1029-15 type 1 specifications.
supported_claims.EV-PU-01#2: Two of the three foams that failed were made with kraft lignin; they failed the compressive strength and/or closed-cell content requirements.
supported_claims.EV-PU-02#1: Rigid foams containing 19-23% (w/w) hardwood kraft lignin, or 25-30% (w/w) organosolv lignin, kept comparable structure and strength.
supported_claims.EV-PU-03#1: Fifteen unmodified lignins (ten kraft, five organosolv) were tested as a replacement for 20 wt% of the petroleum-based polyol in flexible polyurethane foam.
supported_claims.EV-PU-03#3: Organosolv lignins were the most suitable for automotive flexible foam; kraft lignins gave denser, stiffer foams that the authors suggest may suit heavy-duty foams.
supported_claims.EV-PU-04#2: In cited studies, kraft lignin replaced up to about 20% of polyol after oxypropylation, up to 50% when depolymerized and oxypropylated, and up to 100% when liquefied in a bio-based polyol.
supported_claims.EV-PU-04#R1: Modification of kraft lignin: Kraft lignin needs significant treatment (for example oxypropylation, depolymerization, or liquefaction) to reach target properties for polyurethanes.
supported_claims.EV-PU-01#R1: Total hydroxyl value of the lignin: Above 200 mg KOH/g (3.56 mmol/g total OH) is cited as the acceptable range for rigid polyurethane foam production. This is total OH, not phenolic OH, so it is not checked against the feedstock's phenolic OH figure.
supported_claims.EV-PU-03#2: Unmodified lignin reduced foam resiliency: compression set rose to 7-32% against 6% for the control, though it stayed within the standard's limit of below 60%.
supported_claims.EV-PU-04#1: The IEA rates polyurethane uses of lignin (foams, panels, coatings, rubber replacement; kraft, organosolv, and soda lignin) at TRL 6.

applications.statement: Kraft lignin has been studied as a partial replacement for petroleum-based polyols in rigid PUR/PIR foams; laboratory studies report both foams passing specifications and kraft-lignin cases with performance limitations.

Unmodified lignin has also been tested as a partial polyol replacement in flexible polyurethane foam; the researchers suggest kraft-lignin foams may suit heavy-duty uses, while organosolv lignins were most suitable for automotive flexible foam.
A review reports modified kraft lignin in polyurethane studies, including oxypropylation, depolymerization, and liquefaction routes.

target_customers.statement: Rigid-foam producers are an implied customer type for lignin-containing PUR/PIR foam.

Heavy-duty foam applications are a possible target use suggested by the flexible-foam study; automotive flexible-foam applications are discussed, though the study found organosolv lignin most suitable there.

competing_materials.statement: Petroleum-based polyols are the incumbent material that lignin is studied to replace.

qualification_requirements.statement: The rigid-foam study assessed performance against ASTM C1029-15 type 1 specifications; its cited acceptable lignin total-hydroxyl range is above 200 mg KOH/g, which is total OH rather than phenolic OH.
The flexible-foam study reports compression set remained within the standard's limit of below 60%.
Kraft lignin generally requires substantial treatment, such as oxypropylation, depolymerization, or liquefaction, to reach polyurethane target properties.

limitations: The rigid-foam studies are laboratory studies across lignin types; one reports that two of three failing foams used kraft lignin, and another found organosolv lignin performed better than kraft lignin.
The flexible-foam work is laboratory-scale and compared foams against automotive OEM requirements; sulfur odor was not measured in that study.
The reported TRL applies to a broad set of polyurethane uses, not specifically to kraft-lignin foam.
One review was available only as an abstract; the reported modification replacement levels each come from a single cited study.
missing_information: The evidence does not document commercial lignin-polyurethane sales, named buyers, regional demand, current lignin prices, contract terms, or market volumes available to Pinecrest.
No evidence establishes that Pinecrest's wet cake can meet foam formulation, hydroxyl, viscosity, moisture, or performance specifications without additional processing.

market_evidence.rationale: The evidence documents research studies and a review of lignin use, but not industry trials, pilots, development partnerships, or commercial sales of lignin-based polyurethane products.

supported_claims.EV-CM-01#1: Oak Ridge National Laboratory (ORNL) specifications for lignin as a carbon fiber precursor (Baker et al. 2005) set lignin content at 99%, ash below 0.1%, volatiles below 5% at 250 °C, and full removal of particulates larger than 1 µm.
supported_claims.EV-CM-03#1: The GreenLight project raised the TRL of lignin precursor fiber production from 2-3 (proof of concept) to 5 (validated in an industrially relevant environment).
supported_claims.EV-CM-04#2: Hard carbons from kraft lignin (carbonized at 1,200 °C) had higher initial coulombic efficiency than those from sulfonated lignin, which the review attributes to lower ash content.
supported_claims.EV-CM-06#2: Stora Enso announced a EUR 10 million pilot production line for lignin-based anode material, operational in 2021, with scale-up planned in standardized 20 kton manufacturing units.
supported_claims.EV-CM-05#1: Activated carbon has no strict limitations on precursor quality, so lignin too impure for other uses can be converted into it.
supported_claims.EV-CM-02#1: DOE's goal was to cut industrial-grade carbon fiber cost from about $20/lb to a target of $5-7/lb, with mechanical properties suitable for automotive use (250 ksi tensile strength, 25 Msi modulus).
supported_claims.EV-CM-06#1: Stora Enso states that qualification with battery manufacturers and carmakers can take 3 years, and that partnering helps shorten this.
supported_claims.EV-CM-03#2: The modelled production cost of GreenLight lignin-based carbon fiber was EUR 12.6/kg, against about EUR 16/kg estimated for PAN-based fiber; cooperation with existing melt-spinning and carbon fiber plants could lower it to EUR 6.5-7.1/kg.
supported_claims.EV-CM-04#1: A feedstock comparison for sodium-ion battery hard carbon lists lignin at about 300 $/t with a carbon yield above 40%, against anthracite (50-200 $/t, about 90%) and cellulose (1,000 $/t, below 10%).
supported_claims.EV-CM-01#2: A fifth precursor specification was later added: residual carbohydrates below 500 ppm (Baker 2011).
supported_claims.EV-CM-01#R1: Lignin content: Greater than 99% (ORNL precursor specification).
supported_claims.EV-CM-01#R2: Ash content: Below 0.1% by weight (ORNL precursor specification).
supported_claims.EV-CM-01#R3: Residual carbohydrates: Below 500 ppm (Baker 2011). Not mapped to the feedstock's carbohydrate percentage, because the source doesn't state the basis of the ppm figure.
supported_claims.EV-CM-01#R4: Volatile material: Below 5% at 250 °C. The feedstock profile has no volatiles field, so this is not checked.
supported_claims.EV-CM-01#R5: Particulate matter: 100% removal of particulates larger than 1 µm in diameter.
supported_claims.EV-CM-02#R1: Purification of kraft lignin: The kraft lignin examined needed purification before it could be used for carbon fiber.
supported_claims.EV-CM-02#R2: Melt spinnability of softwood lignin: A plasticizing (alloying) agent is needed to melt-spin softwood lignin.
supported_claims.EV-CM-05#3: Higher ash in the lignin lowered activated carbon yield and carbon conversion.
supported_claims.EV-CM-05#R1: Precursor quality: No strict limitations on precursor quality; lower ash improves yield.

applications.statement: Lignin has been investigated as a precursor for carbon fiber, with research describing precursor specifications and lignin-fiber development; a project report says precursor-fiber production reached validation in an industrially relevant environment.
Kraft lignin-derived hard carbon has been studied for sodium-ion battery anodes; lignin-based hard carbon is also described for lithium-ion battery anode materials.
Lignin can be converted into activated carbon, including in a laboratory study using zinc chloride activation.

target_customers.statement: Automotive applications are a potential target for lignin-based carbon fiber, as the cited development work frames fiber properties for automotive use.

Battery-material manufacturers are implied customers for lignin-derived hard carbon used in sodium-ion and lithium-ion batteries; the lithium-ion source specifically refers to qualification with battery manufacturers and carmakers.

competing_materials.statement: PAN-based carbon fiber is a named comparator to lignin-based carbon fiber.
Anthracite is listed as a fossil-precursor comparator for hard-carbon feedstock, and the review also compares cellulose.

qualification_requirements.statement: The cited ORNL carbon-fiber precursor specifications include lignin content greater than 99%, ash below 0.1% by weight, volatiles below 5% at 250 °C, removal of particulates larger than 1 µm, and residual carbohydrates below 500 ppm.
The cited kraft lignin examined for carbon fiber needed purification; softwood lignin also needs a plasticizing agent for melt-spinning.
The hard-carbon battery evidence reports carbonization at 1,200 °C for the compared kraft-lignin material, but does not give a general customer qualification standard.
The activated-carbon study reports no strict precursor-quality limits, while noting that lower ash improves yield and carbon conversion.

limitations: The stringent ORNL precursor specifications apply to carbon fiber, not hard carbon or activated carbon, and are cited secondhand; the study's lignin was not from standard kraft pulping.

The carbon-fiber report is from a 2009 progress report; its measured mechanical properties were below the stated target, and the cited cost values from the later project report are modelled rather than measured.
The GreenLight project report is a project summary rather than an independent review, and its TRL applies to precursor-fiber production, not the entire carbon-fiber chain.

The hard-carbon comparison is a review summarizing other studies and covers sodium-ion batteries; the commercial qualification announcement is company investor material with forward-looking plans as of 2021.
The activated-carbon evidence is a laboratory study using zinc chloride activation.
missing_information: The evidence does not establish current regional demand, lignin purchase prices, named carbon-material buyers, sale volumes, contract terms, or qualification status for Pinecrest lignin.

No carbon-fiber, battery-anode, or activated-carbon test result is reported for Pinecrest's wet cake; the feedstock's missing composition, ash-related screening data, and molecular-weight measurements limit assessment against application-specific requirements.
The evidence does not provide a general hard-carbon or activated-carbon customer qualification standard or current commercial market volumes.

market_evidence.rationale: A project report documents precursor-fiber development to an industrially relevant validation stage, and a company announced a pilot line for lignin-based anode material. The evidence is project/company reporting and does not establish sales to established buyers or several commercial producers.

processing_requirements.statement: Kraft lignin needs activation or depolymerization before use in PF resin; Pinecrest lacks chemical-modification equipment, so this would require new equipment or an external processor.
The mill has no lignin dryer, while moisture is uncertain and the material is wet cake; establish drying and handling requirements before shipment or processing.
Diversion requires replacing the stream's current internal-fuel use.

technical_maturity.statement: A techno-economic comparison reports TRL 9 for LignoBoost extraction combined with phenol substitution in resins (LB+Resin); this is not evidence that Pinecrest's feedstock is qualified.

adoption_barriers.statement: Although a vendor describes industrially proven veneer-plywood resin and reports performance against EN 314-2 Bonding Class 3 and formaldehyde testing under EN 717-2, Pinecrest has no commercial-scale qualification result for its wet cake.
Regional demand, named buyers, prices, accessible volumes, contracts, and qualification timelines are unestablished; plywood and panel producers are the implied customer group.
Molecular-weight data are missing, and the evidence does not establish that Pinecrest cake meets process or product specifications.

The compatibility check returned no score because there were no numeric requirements to compare.

documented_facts.statement: For kraft lignin in phenol-formaldehyde (PF) resins, the typical replacement of phenol is up to 50%, using a two-step process with depolymerized lignin (Mw 800-1,700 g/mol).
Kraft lignin needs an activation or depolymerization step before use in PF resins.
Pre-treatment of kraft lignin: Activation or depolymerization is needed before kraft lignin is used in PF resins.
UPM states that LPF resin is industrially proven and meets EN 314-2 Bonding Class 3 for veneer plywood.
UPM reports formaldehyde emissions (EN 717-2) of 0.230 mg/m²/h for 12 mm spruce, 0.148 for 12 mm birch, and 0.170 for 12 mm combi panels made with LPF resin.
With the depolymerized lignin making up 50% of the phenolic component, the resin's viscosity, bonding strength, and free formaldehyde met the Chinese wood-adhesive standard used in the study.
Global PF resin production was expected to reach about 10 Mt (valued at about USD 13.36 billion in 2019), and more than 50% of these resins are used to make adhesives for wood-based panels.
Replacing 30 wt% of the petroleum-based polyol with unmodified lignin, 16 of the 19 lignins tested gave rigid PUR/PIR foams that passed all measured ASTM C1029-15 type 1 specifications.
Two of the three foams that failed were made with kraft lignin; they failed the compressive strength and/or closed-cell content requirements.
Rigid foams containing 19-23% (w/w) hardwood kraft lignin, or 25-30% (w/w) organosolv lignin, kept comparable structure and strength.
Fifteen unmodified lignins (ten kraft, five organosolv) were tested as a replacement for 20 wt% of the petroleum-based polyol in flexible polyurethane foam.
Organosolv lignins were the most suitable for automotive flexible foam; kraft lignins gave denser, stiffer foams that the authors suggest may suit heavy-duty foams.
In cited studies, kraft lignin replaced up to about 20% of polyol after oxypropylation, up to 50% when depolymerized and oxypropylated, and up to 100% when liquefied in a bio-based polyol.
Modification of kraft lignin: Kraft lignin needs significant treatment (for example oxypropylation, depolymerization, or liquefaction) to reach target properties for polyurethanes.

Total hydroxyl value of the lignin: Above 200 mg KOH/g (3.56 mmol/g total OH) is cited as the acceptable range for rigid polyurethane foam production. This is total OH, not phenolic OH, so it is not checked against the feedstock's phenolic OH figure.
Unmodified lignin reduced foam resiliency: compression set rose to 7-32% against 6% for the control, though it stayed within the standard's limit of below 60%.
The IEA rates polyurethane uses of lignin (foams, panels, coatings, rubber replacement; kraft, organosolv, and soda lignin) at TRL 6.

Oak Ridge National Laboratory (ORNL) specifications for lignin as a carbon fiber precursor (Baker et al. 2005) set lignin content at 99%, ash below 0.1%, volatiles below 5% at 250 °C, and full removal of particulates larger than 1 µm.
The GreenLight project raised the TRL of lignin precursor fiber production from 2-3 (proof of concept) to 5 (validated in an industrially relevant environment).
Hard carbons from kraft lignin (carbonized at 1,200 °C) had higher initial coulombic efficiency than those from sulfonated lignin, which the review attributes to lower ash content.
Stora Enso announced a EUR 10 million pilot production line for lignin-based anode material, operational in 2021, with scale-up planned in standardized 20 kton manufacturing units.
Activated carbon has no strict limitations on precursor quality, so lignin too impure for other uses can be converted into it.
DOE's goal was to cut industrial-grade carbon fiber cost from about $20/lb to a target of $5-7/lb, with mechanical properties suitable for automotive use (250 ksi tensile strength, 25 Msi modulus).
Stora Enso states that qualification with battery manufacturers and carmakers can take 3 years, and that partnering helps shorten this.

The modelled production cost of GreenLight lignin-based carbon fiber was EUR 12.6/kg, against about EUR 16/kg estimated for PAN-based fiber; cooperation with existing melt-spinning and carbon fiber plants could lower it to EUR 6.5-7.1/kg.
A feedstock comparison for sodium-ion battery hard carbon lists lignin at about 300 $/t with a carbon yield above 40%, against anthracite (50-200 $/t, about 90%) and cellulose (1,000 $/t, below 10%).
A fifth precursor specification was later added: residual carbohydrates below 500 ppm (Baker 2011).
Lignin content: Greater than 99% (ORNL precursor specification).
Ash content: Below 0.1% by weight (ORNL precursor specification).
Residual carbohydrates: Below 500 ppm (Baker 2011). Not mapped to the feedstock's carbohydrate percentage, because the source doesn't state the basis of the ppm figure.
Volatile material: Below 5% at 250 °C. The feedstock profile has no volatiles field, so this is not checked.
Particulate matter: 100% removal of particulates larger than 1 µm in diameter.
Purification of kraft lignin: The kraft lignin examined needed purification before it could be used for carbon fiber.
Melt spinnability of softwood lignin: A plasticizing (alloying) agent is needed to melt-spin softwood lignin.
Higher ash in the lignin lowered activated carbon yield and carbon conversion.
Precursor quality: No strict limitations on precursor quality; lower ash improves yield.
A techno-economic comparison lists LignoBoost extraction combined with phenol substitution in resins ('LB+Resin') at TRL 9.
